questions.question: Which equation correctly shows the thermal decomposition of sodium nitrate? A: 2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2; B: 4NaNO3 -> 2Na2O + 4NO2 + O2; C: 2NaNO3 -> Na2O + N2O5; D: 2NaNO3 -> 2Na + 2NO2 + O2
questions.answer: A: 2NaNO3 -> 2NaNO2 + O2
steps: The nitrates of Group 1 metals (except lithium) decompose to the nitrite and oxygen only.
B shows the products of lithium nitrate and of the Group 2 nitrates: the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.
C and D are balanced but are not observed: the metal ion is never reduced to the metal, and N2O5 is not formed.

questions.question: A white solid dissolves in water to give a colourless solution. The solid gives a green flame in a flame test, and the solution gives a white precipitate with dilute sulfuric acid. What is the solid? A: MgCl2; B: CaCl2; C: SrCl2; D: BaCl2
questions.answer: D: BaCl2
steps: Barium compounds give a green (apple-green) flame colour.
Barium sulfate is insoluble, so Ba2+(aq) gives a white precipitate with sulfate ions.
A is wrong: magnesium gives no flame colour. B is wrong: calcium gives a brick-red flame. C is wrong: strontium gives a red flame, although SrSO4 is also a white precipitate.

questions.question: Calcium reacts with cold water. Write the equation for the reaction, including state symbols, and state two observations.
questions.answer: Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g); effervescence and the calcium dissolves, forming a cloudy white suspension
steps: Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g) (correct formulae, balanced, with state symbols)
Any two observations: bubbles of gas (effervescence) and the calcium dissolves or disappears
accept: a cloudy white suspension forms or the solution turns milky (Ca(OH)2 is sparingly soluble)
the solution (or test tube) warms up
Ca(OH)2(s) accepted as the state symbol for calcium hydroxide

questions.question: Lithium carbonate decomposes when heated with a Bunsen burner, but sodium carbonate does not. (i) Write the equation for the decomposition of lithium carbonate. (ii) Explain why lithium carbonate is less thermally stable than sodium carbonate.
questions.answer: (i) Li2CO3 -> Li2O + CO2; (ii) Li+ is smaller, with a higher charge density, so it polarises the carbonate ion more and weakens the C-O bonds
steps: Li2CO3 -> Li2O + CO2
Li+ is smaller than Na+ (same charge), so has a higher charge density and greater polarising power
It distorts the carbonate ion more, weakening the C-O bond, so it decomposes at a lower temperature
accept: state symbols included: Li2CO3(s) -> Li2O(s) + CO2(g)
Li+ has a smaller ionic radius, so a greater attraction for the electrons of the carbonate ion
the carbonate ion is polarised more by Li+ than by Na+

questions.question: Explain why the thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates increases from magnesium carbonate to barium carbonate.
questions.answer: Down the group the cation gets larger, so charge density and polarising power fall, the carbonate ion is distorted less and more energy is needed to decompose it
steps: The ionic radius of the Group 2 cation increases down the group (more shells), with the same 2+ charge
So the charge density of the cation decreases
So the polarising power decreases and the carbonate ion is distorted less
The C-O bond in the carbonate ion is weakened less
More energy (a higher temperature) is needed to decompose the carbonate, so thermal stability increases
accept: decomposition equation such as BaCO3 -> BaO + CO2 given as support
cations with a lower charge density polarise the carbonate ion less
larger cation means a smaller attraction for the oxygen electron cloud of the anion

questions.question: Barium sulfate is swallowed by patients in a "barium meal" before X-rays, but soluble barium compounds are toxic. (a) Explain why barium sulfate is safe to swallow.
questions.answer: Barium sulfate is insoluble in water, so almost no toxic Ba2+(aq) ions are released
steps: Barium ions, Ba2+(aq), are toxic
Barium sulfate is insoluble, so almost no Ba2+ ions are released into solution or absorbed by the body
accept: barium sulfate passes through the digestive system without dissolving
the concentration of dissolved Ba2+ is extremely low
an insoluble compound cannot be absorbed into the bloodstream

questions.question: Barium sulfate can be made by mixing aqueous solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulfate. (b) Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of barium sulfate.
questions.answer: Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s)
steps: Ba2+(aq) + SO4^2-(aq) -> BaSO4(s)
accept: full equation BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq) with state symbols
equation showing the precipitate as BaSO4(s) with Ba2+ and SO4^2- as aqueous ions

questions.question: Magnesium hydroxide is used in some indigestion remedies. A patient has 150 cm^3 of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.0800 mol dm^-3 in the stomach. (c) Calculate the mass of magnesium hydroxide needed to neutralise all of this acid. [Ar: Mg = 24.3, O = 16.0, H = 1.0]
steps: Mg(OH)2 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + 2H2O. Moles of HCl = 0.0800 x 150 / 1000 = 0.0120 mol.
Moles of Mg(OH)2 = 0.0120 / 2 = 0.00600 mol.

questions.question: In the test for sulfate ions, aqueous barium chloride is added to the sample after dilute hydrochloric acid. (d) Explain why the acid is added first.
questions.answer: To remove carbonate (and sulfite) ions, which would otherwise form a white precipitate with barium ions
steps: To remove carbonate ions (and sulfite ions) from the sample
These would otherwise form a white precipitate with barium ions (BaCO3), giving a false positive; BaCO3 dissolves in the acid but BaSO4 does not
accept: acid reacts with carbonate ions, releasing CO2
sulfite ions would give a precipitate of BaSO3
so that only sulfate ions produce a precipitate

questions.question: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium bromide. Which product is NOT formed? A: HBr; B: Br2; C: SO2; D: H2S
questions.answer: D: H2S
steps: Sodium bromide first forms steamy fumes of HBr, which is partly oxidised by the acid to orange-brown bromine, Br2.
The sulfuric acid is reduced from S(+6) to S(+4), forming SO2 (C).
Bromide is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfur further to H2S (S(-2)); that happens only with iodide.

questions.question: A cream precipitate forms when acidified silver nitrate is added to a halide solution. Which statement about this precipitate and aqueous ammonia is correct? A: it dissolves in dilute but not in concentrated ammonia; B: it dissolves in concentrated but not in dilute ammonia; C: it dissolves in both; D: it dissolves in neither
questions.answer: B: it dissolves in concentrated but not in dilute ammonia
steps: A cream precipitate is silver bromide, AgBr.
AgBr is insoluble in dilute ammonia but dissolves in concentrated ammonia, forming the complex ion [Ag(NH3)2]+.
AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia and AgI is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia, so A, C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Chlorine is added to drinking water. (i) Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with water. (ii) State the oxidation numbers of chlorine in the two products. (iii) State why chlorine is added to drinking water.
questions.answer: (i) Cl2 + H2O <=> HCl + HClO; (ii) -1 in HCl and +1 in HClO; (iii) to kill bacteria (disinfect the water)
steps: Cl2 + H2O <=> HCl + HClO
Oxidation number of chlorine: 0 in Cl2, -1 in HCl and +1 in HClO
To kill bacteria (sterilise or disinfect the water)
accept: HOCl written in place of HClO
Cl2 + H2O <=> H+ + Cl- + HClO
chlorate(I) (ClO-) is the oxidising agent that kills micro-organisms

questions.question: A 1.000 g sample of a sodium halide, NaX, is dissolved in water and an excess of aqueous silver nitrate is added. The silver halide formed has a mass of 1.825 g. Calculate the relative atomic mass of X and hence identify X. [Ar: Na = 23.0, Ag = 107.9]
questions.answer: Ar of X = 79.9, so X is bromine
steps: Ag+ + X- -> AgX, so 1 mol NaX gives 1 mol AgX. Let Ar of X = A.
The element with Ar = 79.9 is bromine, so X is Br.

questions.question: At room temperature chlorine is a gas but iodine is a solid. Explain this difference.
questions.answer: I2 has more electrons than Cl2, so stronger London forces between molecules need more energy to overcome
steps: Chlorine and iodine are simple molecules held together by London (dispersion) forces
I2 has more electrons, so a larger electron cloud and stronger London forces than Cl2
More energy is needed to separate I2 molecules, so I2 is a solid while Cl2 is a gas
accept: van der Waals forces or instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces accepted for London forces
the strength of London forces increases with the number of electrons (or the Mr) of the molecule
the covalent bond within the molecules is not broken on melting or boiling

questions.question: A student adds aqueous chlorine to aqueous potassium bromide, then adds cyclohexane and shakes the mixture. (a) Describe what is seen.
questions.answer: The aqueous layer turns orange (bromine forms); the upper cyclohexane layer becomes orange-red
steps: The aqueous solution turns orange (bromine is formed)
The upper cyclohexane layer is orange (or orange-red) because bromine dissolves in it
accept: yellow-orange or brown accepted for bromine in water
orange-red or red-brown accepted for bromine in cyclohexane
two layers form with the colour concentrated in the upper layer

questions.question: Aqueous chlorine reacts with aqueous potassium bromide. (b) Write the ionic equation for the reaction.
questions.answer: Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2
steps: Cl2 + 2Br- -> 2Cl- + Br2
accept: state symbols included: Cl2(aq) + 2Br-(aq) -> 2Cl-(aq) + Br2(aq)
full equation Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2

questions.question: Aqueous bromine is added to aqueous sodium chloride. The electrode potentials are Cl2 + 2e- <=> 2Cl-, E = +1.36 V and Br2 + 2e- <=> 2Br-, E = +1.07 V. (c) Use these data to explain whether a reaction occurs.
questions.answer: No reaction; E cell = -0.29 V, which is negative
steps: E cell is negative, so the reaction is not feasible
Bromine cannot oxidise chloride ions (chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent), so no reaction occurs
accept: E cell for the reverse reaction (Cl2 + 2Br-) is +0.29 V, showing that chlorine displaces bromide
no colour change is observed: the solution stays orange-brown
Cl2 is a stronger oxidising agent than Br2 because its E value is more positive

questions.question: A student has unlabelled solutions of sodium chloride and sodium iodide. (d) Describe a test with silver nitrate and ammonia that distinguishes them, giving the results for each.
questions.answer: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: chloride gives a white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia; iodide gives a yellow precipitate insoluble in concentrated ammonia
steps: Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate, to a sample of each solution
Chloride gives a white precipitate (AgCl) that dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia
Iodide gives a yellow precipitate (AgI) that is insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia
accept: concentrated ammonia added to both precipitates: AgCl dissolves, AgI does not
pale yellow or cream-yellow for silver iodide
ionic equations Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s) and Ag+(aq) + I-(aq) -> AgI(s)

questions.question: Which aqueous ion is colourless? A: Cr3+; B: Fe3+; C: Zn2+; D: Co2+
questions.answer: C: Zn2+
steps: Zn2+ has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d^10, so the 3d subshell is full.
There is no empty d orbital for an electron to be promoted into, so no visible light is absorbed and the ion is colourless.
Cr3+ (3d^3), Fe3+ (3d^5) and Co2+ (3d^7) have incomplete d subshells, so they absorb visible light and are coloured.

questions.question: What is the oxidation state of cobalt in the complex ion [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+? A: +1; B: +2; C: +3; D: +4
steps: NH3 is a neutral ligand and each Cl- ligand has a charge of -1.
Let the oxidation state of Co be x: x + 4(0) + 2(-1) = +1, so x = +3.

A is wrong: it takes the overall charge as the oxidation state and ignores the chloride ligands. B is wrong: it counts only one chloride ligand. D is wrong: it would need the ligands to carry a total charge of -3.

questions.question: Define the term transition metal, and use your definition to explain why zinc is not a transition metal.
questions.answer: A d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d subshell; Zn2+ has a full 3d^10 subshell
steps: A transition metal is a d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell
Zn2+ has a full 3d^10 subshell, so zinc does not form an ion with an incomplete d subshell and is not a transition metal
accept: forms at least one ion with a partially filled d orbital or subshell
zinc forms only the Zn2+ ion, [Ar] 3d^10
zinc atom is [Ar] 3d^10 4s^2, so it also has a full d subshell

questions.question: Zinc is added to an acidic solution containing yellow VO2^+ ions (vanadium in the +5 state). Describe the sequence of colour changes seen as the vanadium is gradually reduced, and give the formula and oxidation state of vanadium in each coloured species.
questions.answer: Yellow VO2^+ (+5), then blue VO^2+ (+4), then green V3+ (+3), then violet V2+ (+2)
steps: Yellow VO2^+ (+5) is reduced to blue VO^2+ (+4)
Blue VO^2+ is reduced to green V3+ (+3)
Green V3+ is reduced to violet V2+ (+2)
accept: oxidation states +4, +3 and +2 given with the correct colours blue, green and violet
names acceptable: dioxovanadium(V), oxovanadium(IV), vanadium(III) and vanadium(II) ions
zinc can reduce vanadium all the way to V2+ because E(Zn2+/Zn) is more negative than each vanadium couple

questions.question: The reaction S2O8^2- + 2I- -> 2SO4^2- + I2 is very slow, but is catalysed by Fe3+(aq). (i) Write two equations showing how Fe3+ catalyses the reaction. (ii) State why transition metal ions can act as catalysts in this way.
questions.answer: (i) 2Fe3+ + 2I- -> 2Fe2+ + I2 and 2Fe2+ + S2O8^2- -> 2Fe3+ + 2SO4^2-; (ii) they have variable oxidation states
steps: Transition metal ions have variable oxidation states (Fe3+/Fe2+), so they can be reduced and then re-oxidised
accept: the two equations given in the other order (Fe2+ oxidised first by S2O8^2-)
iron ions can accept and donate electrons readily
Fe3+ is regenerated at the end, so it acts as a catalyst

questions.question: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is pale blue and turns deep blue when excess aqueous ammonia is added. Aqueous zinc sulfate is colourless. Explain these observations in terms of the electrons in the d orbitals.
questions.answer: Ligands split the d orbitals; d electrons absorb visible light (DeltaE = hv) and the transmitted light is the colour seen; ammonia changes DeltaE; Zn2+ has no gap to excite into
steps: Water ligands split the 3d orbitals of Cu2+ into two energy levels, with an energy gap DeltaE
An electron is promoted between d levels by absorbing visible light of frequency v, where DeltaE = hv
The light that is not absorbed is transmitted, so the solution appears blue (the complementary colour)
Ammonia ligands replace water and change DeltaE, so a different frequency is absorbed and the solution is a deeper blue
Zn2+ has a full 3d^10 subshell, so there is no d-d electron promotion and no visible light is absorbed: colourless
accept: DeltaE = hv = hc/wavelength
the colour seen is the complementary colour to the light absorbed
different ligands cause different splitting of the d orbitals
in an octahedral complex the d orbitals split into a lower set of three and an upper set of two

questions.question: The pink complex ion [Co(H2O)6]2+ reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid to form the blue complex ion [CoCl4]2-. (a) State the coordination number of cobalt and the shape of the ion in [Co(H2O)6]2+.
questions.answer: Coordination number 6; octahedral
steps: 6 (coordination number)
Octahedral
accept: six coordinate (dative) bonds from the water ligands
octahedral with bond angles of 90 degrees

questions.question: The pink complex ion [Co(H2O)6]2+ reacts with concentrated hydrochloric acid to form the blue complex ion [CoCl4]2-. (b) Write the equation for this ligand substitution.
accept: state symbols included
a single forward arrow accepted in place of the reversible arrow

questions.question: In the reaction in (b), the coordination number of cobalt changes from 6 to 4. (c) Explain why only four chloride ligands fit around the cobalt ion.
questions.answer: Chloride ions are larger than water molecules, so fewer can fit around the central ion
steps: Chloride ions are larger than water molecules
So only four chloride ions can fit around the cobalt ion (six would be too crowded)
accept: steric hindrance or repulsion between the chloride ligands
fewer large ligands can fit around the central ion
the chloride ligands carry a negative charge and repel each other

questions.question: Ethane-1,2-diamine, H2NCH2CH2NH2 (en), is a bidentate ligand. [Co(H2O)6]2+ + 3en -> [Co(en)3]2+ + 6H2O is more favourable than [Co(H2O)6]2+ + 6NH3 -> [Co(NH3)6]2+ + 6H2O. (d) Explain this difference in terms of entropy.
questions.answer: The en reaction increases the number of particles from 4 to 7, so entropy increases (DeltaS positive); the NH3 reaction has 7 particles on each side so DeltaS is about zero
steps: With en there are 4 particles on the left and 7 on the right, so the number of particles and the entropy increase (DeltaS positive)
With NH3 there are 7 particles on each side, so DeltaS is approximately zero
The enthalpy changes are similar, so DeltaG = DeltaH - TDeltaS is more negative with en: the chelate effect gives a more stable complex
accept: en is bidentate, so one en molecule replaces two water molecules
greater disorder or more ways of arranging the energy when more particles are formed
a more negative DeltaG means the substitution is more feasible
